This lizard was carefully described by HASSELQUIST, Travels p. 356-358, under this name: Lacerta (Gecko) cauda tereti mediocri, pedibus cristatis, subtus longitudinaliter lamellosis [lizard (gecko) with a moderate, rounded tail, crested feet, lamellate lengthwise underneath]. "The body," he says, "the head and the feet are hairless and smooth. Very small, raised, shining points are scattered over the whole back. Very small pores run along the abdomen. Rather large, soft scales cover the very small space between the loins underneath. The back, head and tail are whitish above, with grey transverse spots scattered irregularly; the throat, abdomen and tail are whitish underneath." From these words it is clear enough that the name leprous was not undeservedly given to this lizard. Now hear the same Hasselquist on the animal's poison, from which it is called سام [sām]. "Most remarkable is this animal's poison, which it exhales from the lobes of its toes. The little animal seeks out places and any things soaked or tinged with sea salt; when it finds such a thing, it runs over it several times, and as it runs it leaves behind it a highly noxious poison. In Cairo, in July 1750, I saw two women and a girl close to death who had eaten fresh salted cheese, bought in the market, on which this little animal had deposited its poison. How acrid the exhalations of its toes are I once saw in Cairo, when the little animal ran over the hand of a certain monk who wanted to catch it: at once, over the whole area the animal had touched, very small pustules arose, with redness, heat and slight pain, exactly as in those who have touched a nettle." FORSKAL also mentions this lizard, in Descriptt. Animall. p. 13: "Lacerta Gecko. By the Egyptians it is called ابو برص [abū baraṣ], i.e. father of leprosy, or leprous; by the people of Aleppo Burs." Schultens, in Comment. ad Proverb. Chapter XXX. vs. 28. p. 486 b, interprets سام ابرص [sām abraṣ] as leprous breather, from سُمَام [sumām], which he says means pestilent blast.

Forskal p. 13: "The origin of the name among the Egyptians is amusing: if it lets its saliva drop into salt intended for use at table, it brings leprosy on the person who tastes it. For this reason they carefully cover the salt-cellar, or add garlic, which the lizard abhors. Others think the animal's name arose from the likeness of its colour to leprosy."
Book 2 of the Canon, ch. 2. عظاية [ʿaẓāya], which the Latin translator omitted.

Hasselquist on the gecko: "Locality: Cairo, where it is very common inside and outside houses." To him should be added Forskal, loc. cit.: "Common in houses at Cairo, roaming over the walls in summer. In winter it is not seen, but is said to hide in the roofs and to come out again in the middle of March."
